title: 150 Companies Back Open-Weight AI as Washington Weighs China Curbs, Nvidia Bets $1.5B on US Packaging, China's Rare-Earth Retaliations Hit Europe
subhead: A coalition of 25 major tech firms publishes a letter defending open-weight AI models as the White House pressures Moonshot AI over alleged chip smuggling and model distillation. Nvidia commits $1.5B to expand US chip packaging with Amkor. China bans exports to 14 EU entities including Rheinmetall, and Indonesia's new rare-earths checks snarl metal shipments.

sections.heading: Tech Giants Circle the Wagons Around Open-Weight AI
sections.body:
A coalition of 25 American technology companies — including Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, IBM, Palantir, Andreessen Horowitz, Hugging Face, and Y Combinator — published a joint letter on July 24 urging Washington to avoid 'premature restrictions on open-weight models.' The letter, titled 'Open Weights and American AI Leadership' and hosted on Microsoft's corporate-responsibility site, argues that US AI leadership depends not on guarding a single best system but on building an open ecosystem that spreads into every sector of the economy.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made his first-ever post on X to amplify the letter, writing that 'open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.' Elon Musk expressed support on X, though neither SpaceX nor Tesla signed. OpenAI and Anthropic did not sign.

The letter makes three claims: open weights widen AI access, sustain competition across chips and clouds, and give customers control over their own data. On the safety argument, the signatories contend that relying on a few closed models creates 'concentrated single points of failure that outsiders cannot inspect,' while open weights let a broad community find vulnerabilities. On distillation — the technique at the center of the Moonshot controversy — the letter calls it 'a widely used technique' that should not be conflated with theft, and that genuine IP violations should be addressed through 'targeted legal and commercial frameworks, not blanket restrictions.'

The timing is deliberate: the letter lands as the Trump administration considers curbs on Chinese open-weight models, and as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 resets expectations for downloadable AI systems. The signatories are pushing back before Washington's instinct hardens into rules. Meanwhile, 179 startups affiliated with the Little Tech Association sent their own letter warning that denying American startups access to models available abroad would 'stifle competition, entrench incumbents, and function as a tax on intelligence.'
sections.whyItMatters: The open-weight debate is no longer academic — it is now a direct lobbying confrontation between the AI industry's largest players, with the outcome shaping whether the US restricts access to Chinese models or lets the market decide.

sections.heading: Washington Escalates Pressure on Moonshot AI as Kimi K3 Stirs the Policy Pot
sections.body:
White House Office of Science and Technology Policy director Michael Kratsios accused Moonshot AI of 'large-scale, covert industrial distillation aimed at stealing proprietary U.S. technology,' claiming the company distilled Anthropic's Fable model to build Kimi K3 and accessed Nvidia GB300 servers in Thailand to train it. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said sanctions and Entity List measures could be considered if distillation crosses into 'IP theft.' The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security is formally investigating Chinese firms over restricted chip use, according to The Information.

Anthropic's public policy executive Sarah Heck backed the allegations, calling theft of American AI models by Chinese firms a 'serious national security risk.' But the accusations are contested: China's embassy spokesperson Liu Chang called the claims 'entirely unfounded,' and several analysts have noted the timeline makes large-scale distillation from newer US models unlikely given Kimi K3's release schedule. Moonshot has denied the claims.

The debate also exposes an internal rift. A Trump official slammed Anthropic on Friday as 'no AI company more hostile to the warfighter,' even though Anthropic had just endorsed the White House's Moonshot allegations. David Sacks, the former White House AI policy chief, pushed back against restrictions on X: 'The Kimi panic needs to stop. President Trump's light-touch regulatory approach is working.' Jensen Huang told Axios that American companies should 'absolutely' be allowed to use Chinese AI models, calling them 'excellent.'

A Reuters analysis noted that the US-China feud over AI safety cooperation is now threatening the very safety efforts both sides claim to prioritize, as each increasingly views frontier AI as a strategic asset that cannot be shared.
sections.whyItMatters: The Moonshot episode is turning into a test case for how the US handles Chinese open-weight models — whether through export controls, sanctions, or leaving the market to decide. The conflicting signals from within the administration itself suggest the policy is far from settled.

sections.heading: Nvidia Commits $1.5B to Amkor for US Chip Packaging Expansion
sections.body:
Nvidia signed a $1.5 billion multi-year agreement with Amkor Technology to expand advanced semiconductor packaging and testing capacity in the United States, as demand for AI infrastructure continues to surge. Under the deal, Nvidia will make a prepayment to support expanded operations including additional capacity at Amkor's Arizona facility. Amkor shares rose 17% in extended trading on the announcement.

Advanced packaging — the process of integrating different semiconductor chips into a single package — has become the bottleneck in AI chip manufacturing. Even as the US has poured over $265 billion into domestic chip production through the CHIPS Act and related programs, a report this week highlighted that the packaging gap remains acute: the US still lacks sufficient domestic capacity for the complex packaging that high-performance AI processors require.

The deal builds on Amkor's existing partnerships with TSMC (a 10-year deal signed in June for US packaging) and AMD. Nvidia's prepayment structure mirrors the capital-intensive nature of packaging infrastructure — no one builds this capacity without guaranteed demand. The agreement also comes as Intel reported its fastest revenue growth in 15 years — $16.1 billion in Q2 2026, up 25.4% year over year — driven primarily by its Data Center and AI business, which grew 59% to $6.3 billion. Intel said it is supply-constrained on data center products, with customers demanding more than it can produce.
sections.whyItMatters: Packaging is the new bottleneck in the AI chip supply chain. Nvidia's $1.5B commitment signals that the biggest AI infrastructure company sees domestic packaging capacity as a strategic necessity, not just a logistics convenience — and that demand continues to outstrip supply.

sections.heading: China's Rare-Earth Retaliations Hit Europe as Indonesia Tightens Checks
sections.body:
China banned the export of dual-use items to 14 additional European Union entities on July 24, with immediate effect. The measures target companies on the cutting edge of chemicals processing, electric motors, and advanced manufacturing, including German defense giant Rheinmetall AG. China's Commerce Ministry said the action was taken in response to EU sanctions related to Russia's war in Ukraine.

The New York Times reported that Beijing is wielding its rare-earths leverage over Europe at a moment when the EU is trying to diversify supply chains away from Chinese critical minerals. The export controls effectively cut off targeted companies from Chinese rare-earth supplies essential for electric motors, catalytic converters, and specialty glass.

Meanwhile, Indonesia's new rare-earths checks are disrupting metal exports. According to Bloomberg, several shipments of alumina and nickel pig iron have been delayed this month as Indonesian customs request additional testing for rare earths and radioactive elements like uranium. Indonesian prosecutors also named suspects in a case involving the illegal export of rare-earth-bearing materials, where lab results were allegedly falsified to obtain export permits. Indonesia has historically leveraged trade measures to promote domestic refining — it banned nickel ore and bauxite exports several years ago, and last year issued a regulation requiring rare earths to be prioritized for domestic use.
sections.whyItMatters: China is demonstrating that rare-earth export controls are a retaliatory tool, not just a precautionary policy. Combined with Indonesia's new checks, the dual disruption is hitting critical mineral supply chains at a time when Europe and the US are trying to reduce dependency — and showing how difficult that actually is.

sections.heading: SpaceX's Starship Deploys First V3 Starlinks as US and China Race in Orbital Servicing
sections.body:
SpaceX's Starship Flight 13 on July 24 achieved several milestones: the second flight of the V3 rocket configuration, the first deployment of 20 upgraded Starlink V3 satellites into suborbital space, and an intact splashdown of the ship — a first for Starship test flights. The Super Heavy booster experienced issues during landing, continuing a pattern of booster recovery challenges. The V3 Starlinks are the most advanced yet, designed for direct-to-mobile service and carrying far greater capacity than earlier generations. The launch came just over two months after the first V3 flight. SpaceX's Starship program carries the weight of NASA's 2028 Artemis moon-landing timeline and a $15 billion bet on orbital capabilities.

Meanwhile, the US launched its most advanced robotic servicing satellite to geosynchronous orbit. Northrop Grumman's Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV), carrying a DARPA-funded RSGS payload with two flexible robotic arms, launched on a SpaceX Falcon 9 on July 22. The $420 million DARPA investment, more than 20 years in development, gives the US a satellite that can inspect, repair, and upgrade satellites that were never designed for servicing — and install Mission Extension Pods on multiple clients. The MRV can also relocate aging satellites, mirroring capabilities China has demonstrated with its Shijian-21 and SJ-25 satellites. US Space Command chief Gen. Stephen Whiting previously warned that China's SJ-21 represents potential offensive counterspace capability. The MRV is the public answer.

On the Chinese side, CAS Space's Kinetica-1 completed its 15th flight on July 24, delivering five commercial satellites to orbit and committing to monthly rideshare launches — a cadence that signals the maturation of China's commercial launch sector.
sections.whyItMatters: Starship's progress toward full reusability and V3 Starlink deployment is commercially and strategically significant for global internet infrastructure. The MRV launch marks the US matching China's orbital servicing capability for the first time — turning geosynchronous orbit into a domain where both sides can now actively manipulate satellites.

sections.heading: AI Safety Cooperation Fractures as US-China Rivalry Intensifies
sections.body:
A Reuters analysis published July 24 detailed how the growing US-China feud over AI is undermining international safety cooperation. As both sides increasingly view frontier AI as a strategic asset and security risk, the channels for sharing safety research and establishing guardrails are narrowing. The White House's push to restrict Chinese models and the Chinese government's rejection of distillation accusations have left little diplomatic room for the kind of technical collaboration that might prevent AI catastrophes.

The fracture is visible on multiple tracks. The US withdrew Anthropic's Fable and Mythos models over security concerns last month. China is considering tighter export controls on AI models and chips, according to a Financial Times report earlier this week. Washington is pressuring allies to restrict Chinese AI systems, while Beijing retaliates with rare-earth export bans. And the proposed Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to cloud-based use of restricted technology, passed the House and awaits Senate action — a bill specifically designed to close the loophole Moonshot allegedly exploited by accessing GB300 servers in Thailand.

The practical effect: researchers on both sides are finding it harder to collaborate on safety benchmarks, red-teaming, and alignment research. A Chinese open-weight model like Kimi K3 can now be downloaded globally, but the US government is weighing whether Americans should even be allowed to use it.
sections.whyItMatters: AI safety requires transparency and cooperation, but the US-China rivalry is actively dismantling both. The risk is not just that one side gets ahead — it's that the guardrails that might prevent catastrophic AI failures go unbuilt because neither side trusts the other enough to share them.

bottomLine: The AI policy fight crystallized this week: 25 major US tech companies publicly lobbied against restricting open-weight models just as the White House escalated accusations of IP theft against Moonshot AI, and the administration's own internal divisions surfaced publicly. Nvidia's $1.5B Amkor deal and Intel's 15-year revenue-growth record both confirm that AI infrastructure demand continues to outstrip supply, while China's rare-earth export bans on EU entities and Indonesia's new mineral checks show that critical mineral supply chains remain a pressure point the West has not yet resolved. In orbit, the US matched China's satellite-servicing capability for the first time with the MRV launch, while SpaceX's Starship V3 hit another milestone — the next frontier of strategic competition is increasingly orbital.
